terms.comment: Traupman gives it for “chatter”; Lewis & Short: “to stammer, stutter”. For chattering teeth Latin says dentibus crepitāre.

evidence: Plaut. Rud. 2.6.52; Lucr. 5.746 (Lewis & Short s.v. crepitō)
terms.comment: Literally “to rattle with the teeth”: dentibus crepitō, my teeth are chattering.

terms.gloss: babble, prate, talk idly and loudly
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Caecil., Afran.; Hor. S.
evidence: Hor. S. 2.7.35: cum magnō blaterās clāmōre (Lewis & Short)
Caecil. ap. Non. 79.2: dēsine blaterāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: colloquial, mostly ante- and post-classical. Plautus has the compound dēblaterō, blab out: quae dēblaterāvistī jam vīcīnīs omnibus (Aul. 268).

phrases.english: we chatter about whatever comes to mind

sources: Lewis & Short: crepito · Lewis & Short: blatero
Lewis & Short: garrio · Lewis & Short: bucca
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 289, 323.
